problems.stem: What distinguishes a wireframe that shows learning logic from one that only shows screen layout?
options: It uses high-fidelity colors and final fonts.
Each region is annotated with the learner action it supports and the moment in the learning sequence it serves, so the layout encodes a teaching decision.
It places the logo and navigation in the expected positions.
It includes every screen the module will ever have.
problems.explanation: A learning-logic wireframe maps regions to learner actions and to where they sit in the instructional sequence. Polish and completeness do not show pedagogical reasoning.

problems.stem: A reviewer says your wireframe is too detailed: it specifies exact pixel widths, final copy, and brand colors. Why is that a problem at the wireframe stage?
options: High fidelity is never useful in instructional design.
Premature visual fidelity pulls review attention to surface choices and discourages changes to the underlying interaction and sequence, which is what the wireframe should still be testing.
Pixel widths are always wrong this early.
Brand colors must be approved by a separate team first.
problems.explanation: Wireframes deliberately stay low-fidelity so reviewers critique flow and learner action, not polish. Over-fidelity locks in the layout before the learning logic is settled.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to generate a wireframe for a practice screen. It returns a polished layout with placeholder feedback shown only after the learner finishes all items. What is the strongest bounded use?
options: Accept the layout because it looks professional and complete.
Use it as a starting block, then move feedback to appear per item if your sequence needs immediate correction, since the tool optimized for appearance, not for the learning interaction.
Reject all AI wireframes and draw everything by hand.
Ask the AI to also decide when feedback should appear and trust its choice.
problems.explanation: AI layouts optimize for plausible appearance, not for the interaction your sequence requires. The designer must place feedback where the learning logic, not the tool, calls for it.

problems.stem: Two wireframes show the same practice screen. Wireframe A places the hint button beside each item; Wireframe B hides all hints behind one button at the bottom. Which annotation would justify choosing B for a mastery-check screen?
options: B looks cleaner with fewer buttons.
On a mastery-check screen the goal is to observe unaided performance, so hints are deliberately made effortful to reach; the layout encodes the assessment intent.
B matches the brand style guide better.
problems.explanation: The right layout depends on the screen's instructional purpose. For a mastery check, making hints harder to reach is a defensible learning-logic decision, not a cosmetic one.
